cue: Hold still, as a frog does. Only things that move show up.
rows: A frog takes little notice of the parts of its world that stay still, and it can starve beside food that never moves. This view shows only what changes, so hold your phone as still as a frog holds itself.
A cane toad can see a light flicker only about 7 times a second, a ninth as often as a person can. Anything that moves smears into a trail.
Field of view, sharpness and pupil
These parts of the view are guesses.

fov.note: one cane toad eye covers nearly 200 degrees and a common frog's two eyes overlap across about 100 degrees; no whole field was found for any one animal, so 300 is a guess

cpd.note: common frog, optomotor test; a leopard frog read 2.8

topoS.note: a horizontal streak of sharp sight is described in treefrogs and the cane toad; how strongly to draw it is the app's choice

fall.note: treefrog best spot 2.1 against periphery 0.9 cycles per degree in air; the ratio 2.33 minus 1

M.note: blue receptor near 433, rod near 502 and red cone near 570 nanometers, taken from toads and a bullfrog; the mapping to camera colors is the app's

gate.note: a still model drew no response in moor frogs, yet frogs also notice large still objects; how far still things fade is a guess

glow.note: how brightly movement stands out is the app's choice

rows: Sharp enough to catch a fly

If you are a common frog, your sharpest vision reaches about 4.3 cycles per degree, measured by how you follow moving stripes. A leopard frog tested with a screen read 2.8. Both are far coarser than a human's.

In a Japanese treefrog the retina holds a horizontal streak of sharp sight close to its equator. Its sharpest spot reaches about 2.1 cycles per degree in air and the lower edge falls to about 0.9. A cane toad and another treefrog also have a streak, so you very likely see a sharp band across the middle with the rest softer by a factor of about 2.3.

A cane toad's eye alone covers nearly 200 degrees, and a common frog's two eyes overlap across about 100 degrees. Nobody has added these up for one animal, so the 300 degrees drawn for you is a guess.

If you are a cane toad, your pupil is horizontal in a black iris with greenish flecks. About 78 of every 100 frog and toad species surveyed have a horizontal pupil, so you very likely do too. A red-eyed treefrog has a vertical one.

A bullfrog's red-sensitive receptor peaks near 570 nanometers. A toad has a second kind of rod, called a green rod, that peaks near 433 in the blue, beside the usual rod near 502. Common toads combine blue receptors with red cones and green rods to tell colors even in dim light, so you very likely read the world as three color signals.

If you are a moor frog, a still model draws no response, and the same model moved up and down a few centimeters does. A common toad reads an object stretched along its path of travel as prey. Nobody has measured how completely a still scene fades for you, so that strength is a guess.
Nobody has measured how brightly a mover stands out against its surroundings for you, or how much blurrier the edge of your streak is than its middle. Those strengths are guesses.

Bullfrog tadpoles feel flowing water through a lateral line, and flows near 1 centimeter per second are close to what they can detect. Frogs hear low and middle pitches from about 50 hertz to 1 kilohertz with one organ of the ear, and some follow smells home. A camera records none of this.
Nobody has measured some parts of how you see, so they are guesses.

rows.title: Speed
rows.text: If you are a cane toad, a light that flashes faster than about 7 times a second looks steady to you, where a human needs about 60 flashes a second before it looks steady. Other Rhinella toads, the cane toad's relatives in the same genus, very likely have a similarly low limit. Nobody has measured it in most other frogs and toads.
rows.note: Only R1 (cane toad, 6.7 Hz) exists; the number is kept to the cane toad and the Rhinella sentence carries only the general ability.

rows.title: Field of view, sharpness and pupil
rows.text: If you are a bullfrog, green frog, northern leopard frog, European common frog or European toad, your pupil is a horizontal almond-shaped slit, though a red-eyed treefrog has an upright one. If you are a northern leopard frog, you see about 3 cycles a degree, about a tenth of the 30 a human reads on an eye chart, and nobody has measured this in most other frogs and toads. Nobody has measured how wide your field of view is.
rows.note: No record gives a field of view for any frog or toad, so the row says so.
